verses.text: The king's order was to be carried out on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar. On that day the enemies of the Jews had hoped to defeat them. But things turned around, and the Jews defeated those who hated them.
The Jews gathered in their cities in all the provinces of King Xerxes to attack those who wanted to harm them. No one could stand against them, because all the peoples were afraid of them.
All the officials of the provinces, the governors, the rulers, and the king's officers helped the Jews, because they were afraid of Mordecai.
Mordecai was very important in the palace. His fame spread all through the provinces, and he became more and more powerful.
The Jews struck down all their enemies with the sword, killing and destroying them. They did whatever they wanted to those who hated them.
In the fortress city of Susa, the Jews killed and destroyed five hundred men.
They also killed Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha,
Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha,
Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai, and Vaizatha,
the ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews. But they did not take any of their property.
That same day the number of people killed in the fortress city of Susa was reported to the king.

The king said to Queen Esther, "The Jews have killed and destroyed five hundred men and the ten sons of Haman in the fortress city of Susa. What must they have done in the rest of the king's provinces! Now what do you want? It will be given to you. What else do you ask? It will be done."
Esther answered, "If it pleases the king, let the Jews in Susa do again tomorrow what today's order allows. And let the bodies of Haman's ten sons be hanged on the pole."
So the king ordered it to be done. An order was announced in Susa, and they hanged the bodies of Haman's ten sons.
The Jews in Susa gathered again on the fourteenth day of the month of Adar, and they killed three hundred men in Susa. But they did not take any of their property.

Meanwhile, the other Jews in the king's provinces also gathered to defend their lives and get rest from their enemies. They killed seventy-five thousand of those who hated them, but they did not take any of their property.
This happened on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar. On the fourteenth day they rested and made it a day of feasting and joy.
But the Jews in Susa had gathered on the thirteenth and fourteenth days, so on the fifteenth day they rested and made it a day of feasting and joy.

That is why the Jews who live in villages and towns without walls celebrate the fourteenth day of the month of Adar as a day of joy and feasting. It is a holiday when they send gifts of food to each other.
Mordecai wrote down these events. He sent letters to all the Jews in all the provinces of King Xerxes, near and far.
He told them to celebrate the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the month of Adar every year.

These were the days when the Jews got rest from their enemies. It was the month when their sadness turned into joy and their mourning into a holiday. He told them to celebrate these days with feasting and joy, sending gifts of food to each other and giving gifts to the poor.
So the Jews agreed to keep on doing what they had started, as Mordecai had written to them.
Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had made a plan to destroy the Jews. He had thrown the pur, which means the lot, to crush and destroy them.
But when the king found out about it, he sent out written orders that Haman's evil plan against the Jews should come back on his own head. So Haman and his sons were hanged on the pole.
That is why these days are called Purim, from the word pur. Because of everything written in Mordecai's letter, and because of what they had seen and what had happened to them,

the Jews decided to make it a custom for themselves, their descendants, and everyone who joined them. Every year, without fail, they would celebrate these two days at the right time, in the way that was written.

These days were to be remembered and celebrated in every generation, by every family, in every province, and in every city. These days of Purim were never to stop being celebrated by the Jews, and their descendants were never to forget them.
Then Queen Esther, daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew wrote with full authority to confirm this second letter about Purim.
Mordecai sent letters with words of peace and truth to all the Jews in the one hundred twenty-seven provinces of the kingdom of Xerxes.

The letters confirmed the days of Purim at their set times, as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther had ordered, and as the Jews had set for themselves and their descendants, including their times of going without food and mourning.
Esther's order confirmed these rules about Purim, and it was written down in the records.
